overview: This file documents Japanese tin production, processing, recycling, and trade between November 1934 and January 1937. Its principal records are Embassy despatches responding to State Department inquiries: a 1934 questionnaire on tin production and shipments, and a detailed 1936 investigation of Japan’s detinning industry, including plant capacities, scrap importers, production figures, and import-export statistics. Cross-reference sheets connect these reports with related material on Kyushu tin deposits, shipments to Japan, Siamese tin-restriction policy, and the Toa Kigyo Corporation’s Yokohama detinning plant. Collectively, the papers show Japan’s dependence on imported tinplate scrap—especially from the United States—alongside expectations that expanding domestic tinplate production and newly exploited deposits would support a more self-sufficient industry.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 1062 on Japanese tin production
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State filing system
subfiles.about: This sheet refers researchers to despatch no. 1062 and its enclosed report on tin production in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's despatch No. 1062 on Japanese tin production, filed at 800.6354/52.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 1062: Questionnaire for Tin Investigation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy submits a preliminary response to a congressional questionnaire concerning Japanese tin production.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to Department instruction no. 625 of October 11, 1934—the OCR misreads the year as 1884—requesting information for a House Foreign Affairs Committee subcommittee. He encloses a short report prepared from information supplied by the Commercial Attaché and states that a more detailed report will follow by later mail.

subfiles.title: Enclosed answers to the tin-investigation questionnaire
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, based on Commercial Attaché information
subfiles.about: This enclosure supplies brief figures and answers concerning tin shipments and an Osaka tin factory.
subfiles.summary: Report gives 1934 tin-ore shipment data (575 tons), describes an Osaka tin factory producing 800 tons yearly under International Tin Committee control.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 1886 on Japan’s detinning industry
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State filing system
subfiles.about: This sheet points to a report on Japanese detinning companies, plant capacity, and expanding domestic tin production.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a 1936 despatch on a 4,500-ton-monthly detinning capacity, crediting new Kyushu deposits for rising Japanese tin output.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 1886: The Detinning Industry in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports on the scale, methods, raw materials, and products of Japanese detinning operations.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1886 reports Japanese detinning plants could treat 4,500 tons of scrap monthly using American-style chemical methods, discussing dependence on imported U.S. tinplate scrap and prospects for a fully domestic industry once domestic tinplate production grows.

subfiles.title: Enclosure no. 1: Companies detinning tin scrap
subfiles.about: This enclosure lists eight Tokyo and Osaka detinning factories and their estimated monthly consumption of tin scrap.
subfiles.summary: Lists eight Tokyo and Osaka detinning plants, totaling 4,500 tons monthly, led by the 1,500-ton Osaka Refined Tin Works.

subfiles.title: Enclosure no. 2: Importers of tin scrap
subfiles.about: This enclosure identifies Japanese firms importing tin scrap and supplies their Tokyo and, where applicable, New York addresses.
subfiles.summary: Lists tin scrap importers Mitsui, Mitsubishi, and Iwai, with Tokyo and New York offices linking Japanese plants to U.S. scrap.

subfiles.title: Enclosure no. 3: Japanese Tin Statistics
subfiles.about: This enclosure tabulates Japanese tin production and trade from 1933 through partial-year 1936.
subfiles.summary: Table shows Japanese tin production rising from 981 to 2,060 tons, 1933-35, with ingot and slab imports far exceeding output.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Singapore despatch no. 57 on tin ore and Siam
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State filing system
subfiles.about: This sheet refers to a Singapore despatch concerning tin-ore shipments to Japan and speculation about Japanese influence on Siam’s tin policy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Singapore despatch on tin ore shipped to Japan, and speculation Japan swayed Siam's tin-restriction stance.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to E. Becker correspondence
subfiles.about: This damaged or badly OCR-corrupted sheet refers to December 1936 correspondence involving E. Becker and a Japanese subject that cannot be recovered reliably.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a garbled E. Becker letter on Japan, filed under 811.6354.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on the Toa Kigyo detinning plant
subfiles.about: This sheet refers to a memorandum containing J. T. Hashimoto’s information on the Toa Kigyo Corporation’s Yokohama plant and other Japanese detinning plants.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a memo on the Toa Kigyo detinning plant in Yokohama and comparable Japanese plants, per J. T. Hashimoto.

subfiles.title: Duplicate cross-reference to memorandum on the Toa Kigyo detinning plant
subfiles.about: This is a duplicate copy of the cross-reference to the memorandum about Toa Kigyo’s Yokohama detinning plant.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cross-reference repeating the memo on the Toa Kigyo detinning plant, again citing J. T. Hashimoto.

interest: Shows Japan's detinning industry, U.S. tinplate-scrap dependence, Kyushu tin mining, and Siam tin-restriction diplomacy, via dispersed State Department filings.
